explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The LORD says to tell Aaron, “Take your staff and throw it down before Pharaoh…” Aaron is Moses’ brother (Exodus 7:2), and Pharaoh is Egypt’s king. No speech, no dance, just drop the stick. Easiest job description I’ve ever heard, and I’ve stamped a crooked cookie or two in my day.

explanations.answer: Strike the palace floor with it
explanations.explanation: Close on the staff part, friend, but that’s not the move here. Striking comes later in this story, and it’s aimed at the Nile. In this scene the LORD says to throw the staff down before Pharaoh, and it will become a serpent (Exodus 7:9). Aaron is Moses’ brother (Exodus 7:2), and nobody’s asked him to bang on any floors.

Nobody is passing the staff to anybody, friend. The LORD says to throw it down before Pharaoh, and it will become a serpent (Exodus 7:9). Pharaoh is Egypt’s king, and the officials are just standing there watching. I think if one of them had been handed that staff, he would have handed it right back.

explanations.answer: Calls his wise men and sorcerers
explanations.explanation: That’s it, baker. Pharaoh “…called the wise men and sorcerers and magicians of Egypt…” He sees a staff turn into a serpent and his first move is to call for backup. That’s like hearing a strange noise from your car and calling your cousin who “knows cars.”

explanations.answer: Sends Moses and Aaron to prison
explanations.explanation: This passage never mentions a prison, friend. What it says is that Pharaoh called the wise men and sorcerers and magicians of Egypt (Exodus 7:11). Moses is Israel’s leader, and Aaron is his brother (Exodus 7:2). The next thing in the story is Pharaoh’s own experts.

explanations.answer: Orders his guards to kill the serpent
explanations.explanation: No guards go after that serpent, friend. The text says Pharaoh called the wise men and sorcerers and magicians of Egypt (Exodus 7:11). So the next move belongs to his experts, not his soldiers. I think the serpent was glad about the guest list for a minute.

True, baker. The text says, “Each one threw down his staff, and it became a serpent.” The wise men, sorcerers and magicians did the same things by their magic arts (Exodus 7:11). Staffs turning into serpents, and then more staffs turning into serpents. I would have needed a minute to sit down.

This one is actually true, friend. The text says the wise men, sorcerers and magicians “…also did the same things by their magic arts.” Then, “Each one threw down his staff, and it became a serpent.” So the magicians’ staffs did turn into serpents too, and that sets up what happens next.

You got it, baker. “But Aaron’s staff swallowed up the other staffs.” Every magician threw down a staff, and one serpent was left standing. I’d have been counting my fingers afterward just to be sure I still had all of them.

Nice try, friend, but nobody gets turned back into wood here. “But Aaron’s staff swallowed up the other staffs.” (Exodus 7:12) Every magician threw down a staff, and it became a serpent. Then Aaron’s staff swallowed up the rest. I think those magicians were doing some quick math about how their morning was going.

explanations.answer: Chases them out of the palace
explanations.explanation: No chase scene in this one, friend. The text says Aaron’s staff swallowed up the other staffs (Exodus 7:12). Nobody is running anywhere in that verse. Sorry to take the action movie away from you.

You got it, baker. “Still, Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, just as the LORD had said.” Pharaoh is Egypt’s king, and he had just seen Aaron’s staff swallow up the other staffs. That's a lot to see and still not listen. I'd have been asking for a replay, and his mind was already made up.

I understand wanting that, friend, but the text says the opposite. “Still, Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them…” Nothing softened in that room. The writer adds that it went “…just as the LORD had said.”

I can see why you’d guess that after serpents showed up, friend. But the text doesn’t say Pharaoh’s heart was troubled. It says his heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, just as the LORD had said (Exodus 7:13). Whatever he felt, that’s what the passage tells us.

explanations.answer: On the bank of the Nile
explanations.explanation: That’s the spot, baker. The LORD tells Moses, “Wait on the bank of the Nile to meet him…” Pharaoh is walking out to the water that morning, so Moses is told to be there when he comes. Moses is Israel’s leader, and I think he’s the only one in Egypt with a morning appointment like that.

Goshen doesn’t come up anywhere in this passage, friend. The LORD says to go to Pharaoh in the morning as he’s walking out to the water, and to wait on the bank of the Nile to meet him (Exodus 7:15). So Moses is waiting at the river. Pharaoh is Egypt’s king, and he’s the one who’s heading to the water.

explanations.answer: At the edge of the Red Sea
explanations.explanation: The Red Sea isn’t mentioned in this passage, friend. Moses is told to wait on the bank of the Nile to meet Pharaoh (Exodus 7:15). Pharaoh, Egypt’s king, is walking out to the water that morning. Same water, just not the one you picked.

True, baker. The LORD says, “…take in your hand the staff that was changed into a snake.” It’s the very same staff that became a serpent in front of Pharaoh. I’d be holding it a little more carefully than usual.

This one is actually true, friend. The LORD tells Moses, “…take in your hand the staff that was changed into a snake.” So it’s the very same staff that became a serpent before Pharaoh. The one that swallowed up the other staffs is the one he brings.

explanations.answer: So they may worship Him in the wilderness
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The LORD’s message says, “Let My people go, so that they may worship Me in the wilderness.” So the reason is worship, and it’s the LORD’s own word. The next line adds that until now Pharaoh has not listened.

explanations.answer: So they may build Him a great temple
explanations.explanation: That’s a good-sounding idea, friend, but this passage doesn’t say it. The LORD says, “Let My people go, so that they may worship Me in the wilderness.” Worship is the reason given in the text. No building plans have been handed out yet.

explanations.answer: So they may rest from all their work
explanations.explanation: Rest would sound great on a Monday, friend, but that isn’t the reason the text gives. The LORD says, “Let My people go, so that they may worship Me in the wilderness.” Worship is the reason, in the LORD’s own words (Exodus 7:16). Pharaoh is Egypt’s king, and this message is for him.
That’s the first blank, baker. “The fish in the Nile will die…” The LORD says it ahead of time, and then it happens in verse 21. I think this one is heavy, and it’s worth sitting with for a second.

You got it, baker. “…the Egyptians will be unable to drink its water.” Think of how many mornings start with a cup of something, and imagine the river itself saying no. The river is the thing they depend on, and it won’t work.
Nice try, friend, but that’s the opposite direction. The LORD says the fish in the Nile will die (Exodus 7:18). Nothing in the verse is multiplying. Let’s save that word for a batch of cookies.

Crossing isn’t what the verse is about, friend. It says the river will stink and the Egyptians will be unable to drink its water (Exodus 7:18). Nobody’s mentioned crossing anything. The trouble is the water itself.

No selling in this verse, friend. The LORD says the Egyptians will be unable to drink the water (Exodus 7:18). It’s about what’s in the river, not about trading anything. I think nobody in Egypt would have bought that water anyway.

True, baker. The LORD says, “There will be blood throughout the land of Egypt, even in the vessels of wood and stone.” So it’s not just the river. It reaches the containers where people keep water too. Even my biggest mixing bowl wouldn’t be safe from that.

This one is actually true, friend. The LORD says, “There will be blood throughout the land of Egypt, even in the vessels of wood and stone.” So it reaches past the river, into the vessels people use. That’s how far the LORD says it will go.

You got it, baker. The text says Aaron raised the staff and struck the water “in the presence of Pharaoh and his officials…” Pharaoh is Egypt’s king, and the officials are with him. Nobody could say they didn’t see it.

Guards would make sense on a riverbank, friend, but the text names someone else. Aaron struck the water in the presence of Pharaoh and his officials (Exodus 7:20). Pharaoh is Egypt’s king. No guards are mentioned in this scene.

Sons aren't named in this scene, friend. The text says Aaron raised the staff and struck the Nile “in the presence of Pharaoh and his officials…” (Exodus 7:20). Pharaoh is Egypt’s king. So the people the text puts right there are the king’s own officials, front row, no way to say they missed it.

I get why you’d think so, friend, but the text says otherwise. “But the magicians of Egypt did the same things by their magic arts.” So they matched it. And that’s why Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he would not listen to Moses and Aaron, just as the LORD had said.

That’s it, baker. The text says, “But the magicians of Egypt did the same things by their magic arts.” So they did match it. Then Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he would not listen to Moses and Aaron, just as the LORD had said.

explanations.answer: Goes into his palace without taking it to heart
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. “Instead, Pharaoh turned around, went into his palace, and did not take any of this to heart.” He had just seen the whole river turn to blood and went straight inside. I think that’s the quietest walk back to a building in the whole Bible.

explanations.answer: Stays on the riverbank to watch the water
explanations.explanation: No, friend, Pharaoh doesn’t stick around. The text says he turned around and went into his palace (Exodus 7:23). Pharaoh is Egypt’s king, and he walked away from the river. He did not take any of this to heart.

explanations.answer: Sends all his officials out to clean the Nile
explanations.explanation: Cleanup isn’t in this passage, friend. What the text says is that Pharaoh turned around, went into his palace, and did not take any of this to heart (Exodus 7:23). Pharaoh is Egypt’s king. Nobody gets sent with a mop.

explanations.answer: They dig around the Nile for it
explanations.explanation: That’s it, baker. “So all the Egyptians dug around the Nile for water to drink, because they could not drink the water from the river.” ALL of them, digging, staring at the ground like it owes them something. I think that's what it looks like when nobody has a backup plan.

Rainwater isn't in the text, friend. It says the Egyptians dug around the Nile for water to drink, because they could not drink the water from the river (Exodus 7:24). No jars lined up, no clouds mentioned. I'd have grabbed a jar and hoped too, but this verse has digging, not weather.

explanations.answer: They buy it from passing traders
explanations.explanation: No traders show up in this passage, friend. The text says all the Egyptians dug around the Nile for water to drink (Exodus 7:24). Buying isn’t mentioned anywhere in the verse. The Egyptians do the digging themselves.
